title: Burns: initial assessment and fluid resuscitation (India)
specialty: Emergency Medicine / Plastic and Burns Surgery / Paediatrics / Critical Care

evidenceAudit.scope: Thermal burns in adults and children in India from first aid to the first 48 hours: cooling, primary survey and inhalation injury, total body surface area (TBSA) estimation, fluid resuscitation, urine output targets, analgesia, tetanus, wound care, escharotomy and referral, built on the DGHS Standard Treatment Guidelines for Management of Burns (2025).
findings: Rule of nines, Lund and Browder and palm rule; fluid resuscitation for adult burns above 15% and child burns of 10% or more; modified Parkland 3 mL/kg/%TBSA and modified Brooke 2 mL/kg/%TBSA Ringer lactate, half in 8 hours; paediatric 2 mL/kg/%TBSA plus maintenance; urine targets 0.5–1 mL/kg/h (adults) and 1 mL/kg/h (children); oxygen SpO2 92–95%; tetanus toxoid 0.5 mL IM; 1% silver sulfadiazine; escharotomy; no routine prophylactic antibiotics; referral levels checked against the DGHS Burns STG (2025).
Cooling with 20 minutes of cool running water within 3 hours and dark-urine target 1–2 mL/kg/h from the New Zealand National Burn Service guideline (2023).
Urine-output fluid challenges from the COBIS adult burns guideline.
Morphine doses from the US label (adults) and the Gloucestershire children's analgesia guideline.
unverifiedSections: The DGHS STG gives no opioid doses; morphine doses come from the US label and a UK children's guideline.
Adult IV resuscitation threshold: DGHS above 15% TBSA; New Zealand above 20%. The Indian threshold is used.
Rule of nines percentages are in a DGHS figure, not text; standard values are shown.
Drug cautions, contraindications and renal or hepatic adjustment lines without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.

pathophysiology.summary: Burns are a major cause of injury in India, especially among women (kitchen and kerosene fires) and children (scalds). Early care decides survival: stop the burning process, cool the wound with running water, assess the airway for inhalation injury, estimate TBSA and depth, start Ringer lactate by formula for large burns, and titrate to urine output rather than the formula alone. Pain relief should be intravenous in the acute phase. Prophylactic antibiotics are not used. Patients meeting referral criteria — large or full-thickness burns, special areas, inhalation, electrical or chemical injury, extremes of age — go to a burns unit.
keyMechanisms: Heat causes coagulative necrosis surrounded by zones of stasis and hyperaemia; cooling limits progression.
Capillary leak in burns above about 15% TBSA causes hypovolaemic burn shock in the first 24 hours.
Smoke causes upper airway oedema, chemical pneumonitis, and carbon monoxide or cyanide poisoning.
Circumferential full-thickness eschar restricts breathing or limb circulation.

physicalSigns: Erythema, blisters (superficial and partial thickness); white or leathery painless skin (full thickness)
Facial burns, soot in the mouth, carbonaceous sputum, wheeze (DGHS STG)
redFlags: Stridor, hoarseness, facial and neck burns: early intubation (DGHS STG)
Enclosed-space fire, reduced consciousness: carbon monoxide poisoning (DGHS STG)
Electrical burns: cardiac monitoring and compartment syndrome
Unexplained burns in a child: safeguarding

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: History; scalds are often partial thickness.
Small skin wounds with deep tissue damage.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Rule of nines (adults), Lund and Browder (children), palm with fingers about 1% for small burns.
Adults above 15% TBSA; children 10% or more.
Deep partial thickness above 40%; full thickness above 10%; inhalation; electrical with vascular compromise; special areas; polytrauma.

clinicalManagement.title: First aid
actions: Stop the burning; cool with cool running water for 20 minutes, within 3 hours (NZ NBS).
Keep the patient warm; cover with cling film or clean sheet (NZ NBS).

clinicalManagement.title: Primary survey
actions: Airway: early intubation for stridor, facial and neck burns or inhalation (DGHS STG).
Oxygen to SpO2 92–95%; high-flow oxygen 8–15 L/min for at least 6 hours if carbon monoxide suspected (DGHS STG).
Two large-bore IV lines; weigh the patient (DGHS STG).

clinicalManagement.title: Fluid resuscitation
actions: Adults above 15% TBSA: Ringer lactate 3 mL/kg/%TBSA (modified Parkland) or 2 mL/kg/%TBSA plus maintenance (modified Brooke); half in 8 hours, half in 16 hours (DGHS STG).
Children 10% or more: Ringer lactate 2 mL/kg/%TBSA plus maintenance (4-2-1 mL/kg/h) (DGHS STG).
Adults under 15%: oral fluids at least 2 L (DGHS STG).
Titrate to urine output; fluid challenge 250 mL if output 0.25–0.5 mL/kg/h (COBIS).

clinicalManagement.title: Pain, tetanus and wound
actions: IV opioid for severe pain; avoid IM injections in shock (DGHS STG).
Tetanus toxoid 0.5 mL IM if not already given (DGHS STG).
1% silver sulfadiazine or silver dressings; leave small blisters; no routine antibiotics (DGHS STG).
Escharotomy for circumferential full-thickness chest or limb burns (DGHS STG).

clinicalManagement.title: Refer
actions: Use DGHS referral criteria to secondary or tertiary burns care (DGHS STG).

regimens.dose: 3 mL × weight (kg) × %TBSA over 24 hours (modified Parkland); half in the first 8 hours, half in the next 16 hours
regimens.frequency: Continuous; titrate hourly to urine output
regimens.duration: First 24 hours; colloid may be added in the second 24 hours
adjustments: Paediatric: Adult topic; paediatric use is outside the scope of the cited sources.
Penicillin allergy: Not an antibiotic; penicillin allergy does not change this medicine.
CKD: Titrate carefully to output; risk of overload in kidney failure.
CLD: Lactate clearance may be reduced; monitor lactate.
Alternative modified Brooke: 2 mL/kg/%TBSA Ringer lactate plus 2500 mL dextrose-saline maintenance (DGHS STG).

regimens.dose: Adults 0.1–0.2 mg/kg IV every 4 hours as needed, given slowly and titrated
adjustments: Paediatric: Children 1–12 years 0.1–0.2 mg/kg IV; 6–12 months 0.1 mg/kg; under 6 months 0.025–0.05 mg/kg; titrate after 5–10 minutes (Gloucestershire guideline).
Penicillin allergy: Not an antibiotic; penicillin allergy does not change this medicine.
CKD: Reduce dose and interval in kidney failure (metabolite accumulation).
CLD: Reduce dose in liver failure; may precipitate encephalopathy.
Paediatric doses: glosan, section IV morphine.

regimens.dose: Adults 1 g; children 15 mg/kg (oral loading 20 mg/kg)
adjustments: Paediatric: Children 15 mg/kg every 4–6 hours, maximum 60 mg/kg/day IV (10–50 kg) or 90 mg/kg/day oral, not above 4 g/day (Gloucestershire guideline).
Penicillin allergy: Not an antibiotic; penicillin allergy does not change this medicine.
CKD: No adjustment usually.
CLD: Reduce to maximum 2 g/day in liver disease.
Paracetamol is listed for burn pain in the DGHS STG (Chapter 7).

medicationPlan.note: Fluid formulas, thresholds, tetanus and wound care from the DGHS Burns STG (2025); opioid doses from the US label and a UK children's guideline because the DGHS STG gives none. India-only topic; the Saudi topic is unchanged. Not clinically reviewed.

teaching.scope: First 48 hours of burn care in Indian hospitals.
learningObjectives: Cool, assess airway and estimate TBSA.
keyPoints: Ringer lactate 3 mL/kg/%TBSA (adults above 15%); children 2 mL/kg/%TBSA plus maintenance.
Titrate to urine output, not the formula.
pitfalls: Missing inhalation injury or carbon monoxide.
